title: Architects don't compete with others, only with a hundred versions of themselves
dek: She says she never felt like she was racing the rat race because she had no one to race against in the first place—architect Qi Shanshan's (戚山山) vitality doesn't come from self-discipline, but from asking herself first whether she actually likes something before deciding to do it.
why: This episode's information density is moderate—it's more a complete showcase of one person's lifestyle. But two points of conversation are worth pausing to reflect on your own decision-making: the logic of wanting-it-all versus choosing what you truly want, and the concept of playing it safe.
who: Entrepreneurs and professionals who plan their lives using the logic of ‘hard work plus fixing weaknesses’ but have a nagging sense something's off, looking for a different frame of reference.

points.h: Female team members, measuring with their bodies, built truer than blueprints
points.body: The construction site of the Tengchong An zhi Ruo Su project was staffed almost entirely by women from the village. They threw bricks up along more than thirty meters and over one hundred steps, relaying materials up the stairs. Qi Shanshan discovered the villagers couldn't read blueprints, so she told them: ‘Listen to your body—turn when your body tells you to.’ They laid bricks by feel. When finished and checked against the blueprints, it was nearly identical. The sections built precisely according to specification, by contrast, looked stiff and lacked spirit.

points.h: Brilliance comes from deviation and error, never from mere precision
points.body: She says she's always fought against the rigid rule of ‘must be perfectly horizontal and vertical.’ Why must stairs go straight up, then make a 180-degree turn? No one walks that way—mountain paths are walked on a slant. She believes all the beautiful moments come from error, deviation, misalignment—from the non-dogmatic places, not from precision itself. Refined technique is the foundation, but what truly moves people comes from respecting nature's irregularity, not from rules imposed by people.

points.h: Fear you direct at yourself is more powerful than external punishment
points.body: Her father disciplined her harshly: he'd strike her fingers when she played a wrong note, beat her even for a score of 99 out of 100, saying it was an attitude problem. After she moved to the US at 14, she finally escaped direct supervision. But she wrote her father's name on a piece of paper and taped it on her desk. Whenever she thought of getting up to play, she'd see the name and scare herself back into studying. She'd transformed his external strictness into a self-monitoring mechanism she maintained herself, not into simple consequence-free abandon.

points.h: How you carry yourself determines what energy the world sends back
points.body: Her mother was a dancer. Caring for several elderly relatives and her injured father at once, physically depleted to the point of collapse, ‘she stood right up, took a lipstick from her pocket, applied it, and went back to work’—because ‘no one was watching.’ Her logic: if you go to work without makeup and looking miserable, people see you as pitiful, and the feedback they send you is negative energy. With lipstick on, they see vitality, and the feedback that comes back is positive energy. ‘So in our family it became the norm: don't complain, don't spiral—and happiness just naturally follows.’

points.h: Working all night for satisfaction is different from racing against others
points.body: Harvard's architecture program kept her working from 9 AM to 5 AM. When tired, she'd run for half an hour and come back to keep working. She completed her degree before the phrase ‘racing the rat race’ became common, and she never felt like she was doing it. Knocking off at 5 AM, even exhausted, she was happy—she'd stopped actively because she was satisfied, not because she was forced to. She says those years didn't train her in design skills, but in ‘how to find satisfaction.’

points.h: One hundred meters of dining hall became the seed of rural transformation
points.body: In a poor village deep in the Qinling Mountains near Hanzhong, girls couldn't attend school because their families couldn't afford lunch fees. The school found a solution: join the soccer team, get free lunch. With no construction land available, the team converted a narrow hundred-meter-long old stable into a cafeteria, using food-service practices from train cars to have children line up in two queues. The team later made it to the provincial squad. The training camp brought parents for coaching, creating needs for housing and hotels, which drove expansion of the fields, reconstruction of the primary school, and a visitor center. Over six or seven years, one cafeteria rolled into complete rural revival, driven by a group of young girls who had no idea they'd changed their village.

points.h: Rest you've approved but don't actually want isn't rest, it's procrastination
points.body: The host reflected on her habit of thinking ‘I have this already—how do I add that to it?’ Qi Shanshan pointed out: this is playing it safe. You've approved downtime and fitness as ‘wonderful things’ in your head, but they're not things you actually want to do, which is why they're at the bottom of your to-do list, not the first thing you want to do when you wake up. Her logic isn't wanting-it-all—it's: ‘What do I actually love doing most?’ Then put that first in your day.

points.h: AI makes renderings beautiful; humans do the work clients actually need
points.body: She doesn't oppose using AI—when she and her colleagues learned architecture twenty years ago, the parametric design they used was already a programming tool. What she opposes is blind hope—outsourcing all the analysis and thinking you should be doing yourself to AI, then not using the time saved to do something more valuable. She says the truly irreplaceable work is face-to-face communication with clients: where is their confusion, what do they want to become? That's deep work requiring you to feel the relationship between people and space on site. AI in the studio handles only surface-level work: making renderings beautiful.

terms.def: Choosing options with high certainty and low risk, rather than acting on your instinctive passion.

quotes.text: I've actually been playing it safe the whole time. My default thinking is: I already have this—how do I add that to it?
All the beautiful things—of course the foundation has to be there, you need refined skill—but all these highlights come entirely from error, deviation, misalignment.
She stood right up, took a lipstick from her pocket, applied it, and went back to work.
So in our family it became the norm: don't complain, don't spiral—and happiness just naturally follows. Whatever troubles come up, you just let them drift away.
I say freewheeling creativity—it's built on a foundation of rigor. Only then can you truly be freewheeling. Without that rigor, you're just messy. That's not expressive, that's chaos.
She said: Shanshan, take three months off or half a year.
My way isn't wanting it all—it's: I want this one thing. It's about discovering yourself.
